questions.question: 19.2% of this IPO's money is an offer for sale. Where does that part of the money go?

choices.text: Into the company, to build new factories.
To the existing owners who are selling their shares.

questions.explanation: In an offer for sale, existing owners sell shares they already hold, so the money goes to them. Only the fresh issue, ₹27.91 crore here, reaches HGS (India) Limited.

numbers.label: Share of the IPO money going to sellers

questions.question: Sales went from ₹35.48 crore in FY24 to ₹45.16 crore in FY26, which is 12.8% a year. How would you describe that?
questions.explanation: 12.8% a year is slow growth: HGS (India) Limited is growing, but not by much.

questions.question: HGS (India) Limited owes 0 rupees of loans for every rupee of its owners' money. Which is closest to the truth?

choices.text: Its loans are small to manageable next to what the owners have put in.
Its loans are heavy: lenders have more riding on it than its owners.
Loans never matter for a company that makes a profit.

questions.explanation: At 0 rupees of loans per rupee of owners' money, HGS (India) Limited's owners have more in the business than its lenders.

questions.question: Big institutions asked for 137.9x the shares kept for them. Why do people watch this figure?

choices.text: Professionals who studied the company closely are showing how keen they are.
It guarantees the share price will rise on listing day.
It tells you how many shares you will be given.

questions.explanation: Institutions do the most homework, and they asked for 137.9x their quota of HGS (India) Limited: strong appetite. Still, no figure guarantees a listing gain.
